topic: How 'Weaponized Light' Lasers Are Vaporizing Drone Swarms
angle: Examine the extreme cost-asymmetry of modern warfare—why militaries are ditching million-dollar missiles to swat $500 plastic drones, and how focused directed-energy lasers melt incoming threats out of the sky for pennies per shot.
why: Anti-drone technology shorts have exploded in viewership over the past week (e.g., recent anti-drone tech videos racking up over 1 million views), proving high audience appetite for next-gen defense explainers. This fresh directed-energy breakthrough provides a compelling physics and cost breakdown that hasn't been saturated on Shorts yet.
facts: Cheap autonomous drones and loitering munitions costing as little as $500 to $2,000 have fundamentally upended modern battlefield air defense.
Traditional base air defenses rely on interceptor missiles that often cost between $300,000 and $2 million each, creating an economically unsustainable defense model against swarms.
Defense contractor KBR has rolled out a new base defense technology centered on high-energy lasers termed 'weaponized light' specifically designed to counter drone threats.

Directed-energy systems fire concentrated photons that travel at the speed of light (approximately 300,000 kilometers per second), completely eliminating the need to calculate target lead or bullet drop.
The laser delivers intense thermal energy onto a tight focal point, melting through drone composite hulls, burning lithium batteries, or severing aerodynamic control surfaces in 1 to 3 seconds.
Targeting optics on high-energy laser systems can also blind or melt the optical and infrared cameras of incoming drones before they reach visual range.
A single shot from a directed-energy laser costs roughly $1 to $10 in electrical power, compared to the astronomical cost of kinetic munitions.
Unlike missile batteries with limited launch tubes, a laser weapon has a virtually 'infinite magazine,' limited only by generator fuel and onboard cooling capacity.
The U.S. military announced the creation of Task Force Easy to accelerate the testing, adaptation, and field deployment of counter-drone technologies.
Environmental conditions like heavy rain, dense fog, and battlefield smoke still pose physical challenges by scattering laser energy before it hits targets.
Engineers are actively developing advanced adaptive optics and thermal management systems to ensure laser weapons can sustain rapid, multi-target engagements during mass swarm attacks.
